missions/chinese-indigenous-church/name: Chinese indigenous and house churches (Watchman Nee, John Sung, Three-Self, Back to Jerusalem)
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/statu: Active but divided between the state-registered Three-Self/China Christian Council churches and a large, diverse unregistered house-church sector. Since 2018 tighter religious regulations and a ‘sinicisation’ campaign have closed prominent urban congregations and restricted online and youth ministry.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/summa: From the early twentieth century Chinese Christians sought to free their churches from missionary control and foreign stigma. Independent churches, the True Jesus Church, the Jesus Family and Watchman Nee’s ‘Little Flock’ (Local Churches), the revival preaching of John Sung and the uncompromising Wang Mingdao created a Chinese Protestantism that survived the expulsion of missionaries after 1949. The Communist state organised the Three-Self Patriotic Movement in 1950–54; those who refused it formed the house churches, which endured the Cultural Revolution and grew after 1979 into one of the largest Christian populations in Asia, with a visionary if largely unrealised ‘Back to Jerusalem’ missionary dream.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/story:
Chinese Protestantism was born under the shadow of the unequal treaties, and many Chinese saw Christianity as a foreign religion protected by gunboats; the Boxer violence of 1900, in which tens of thousands of Chinese Christians and some two hundred missionaries were killed, sharpened the question of whether Chinese believers could own their faith. In 1906 Yu Guozhen founded the Chinese Christian Independent Church in Shanghai, and by the 1920s hundreds of self-supporting congregations had joined it. The National Christian Conference of 1922, the founding of the Church of Christ in China (1927) and the anti-Christian movement of 1922–27 made ‘indigenisation’ the watchword of Chinese Protestant leaders such as Cheng Jingyi.

More radical independence came from below. In Beijing in 1917 Wei Enbo, influenced by Pentecostal missionaries, founded the True Jesus Church, Sabbath-keeping, baptising in Jesus’ name and practising tongues and healing. In Shandong, Jing Dianying founded the Jesus Family at Mazhuang in the 1920s, a communal society of shared property and ecstatic worship. In Fuzhou the young Ni Tuosheng (Watchman Nee), shaped by Plymouth Brethren teaching and the missionary Margaret Barber, rejected denominations altogether; his ‘local churches’ (called the Little Flock by others) recognised one church per city, and his writings such as The Spiritual Man and The Normal Christian Life later became evangelical classics in the West. Wang Mingdao’s Christian Tabernacle in Beijing (from 1925) stood for strict biblicism and complete self-support.

Revival gave this movement fire. The Norwegian Lutheran missionary Marie Monsen’s searching preaching helped spark the Shandong Revival (1927–37), with its confession of sin, healings and spiritual gifts. The American-educated chemist John Sung (Song Shangjie), returning in 1927, became China’s most famous evangelist: with the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band from 1931, and then alone, he preached in almost every province and from 1935 among the Chinese of the Philippines, Singapore, Malaya, Siam, Indonesia and Taiwan, leaving behind thousands of witness teams. These revivals planted an evangelical, conversion-centred piety that proved independent of missionaries.

After 1949 the new government required churches to sever foreign ties. The ‘Christian Manifesto’ drafted by Wu Yaozong (Y. T. Wu) with Zhou Enlai’s approval in 1950 launched the Three-Self Patriotic Movement, formally organised in 1954, which borrowed the old missionary slogan of self-government, self-support and self-propagation for a new political purpose. All foreign missionaries had left by the early 1950s. Accusation meetings denounced missionaries and Chinese leaders; Wang Mingdao, refusing to join, was imprisoned from 1955 to 1979; Watchman Nee was arrested in 1952 and died in a labour camp in 1972; Catholic bishops loyal to Rome were jailed. In the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) all public worship ceased, but Christians met secretly in homes, especially in rural Henan, Anhui and Zhejiang.

When churches reopened in 1979 the Christian community was far larger than in 1949, when there had been perhaps 700,000–1 million Protestants. The China Christian Council (1980), led by Bishop K. H. Ting (Ding Guangxun), worked with the Three-Self Movement to reopen churches, train pastors and print Bibles through the Amity Press (from 1987). Alongside it grew vast unregistered networks, among them the Fangcheng fellowship, China Gospel Fellowship, the Born Again movement of Xu Yongze and the house churches of Wenzhou, while urban leaders such as Allen Yuan and Samuel Lamb (Lin Xiangao) in Guangzhou became symbols of faithful endurance. Estimates of Chinese Protestants in the 2010s range from the government’s 38 million (2018) to Pew’s c. 58 million (2010) and higher figures from some advocates, figures that reflect real uncertainty.

The Back to Jerusalem vision began in the 1940s, when Chinese evangelists from the Northwest Bible Institute at Fengxiang and the Jesus Family’s Northwest Spiritual Band set out to evangelise westward through Xinjiang toward the Muslim world and ultimately Jerusalem; their leaders, including Mark Ma and Simon Zhao, were stopped by the Communist victory, and Zhao spent decades in prison. Revived in the 2000s through the books of Brother Yun (Liu Zhenying) and Paul Hattaway, with an announced goal of 100,000 missionaries, the vision has mobilised Chinese mission interest but produced far smaller numbers than proclaimed. Since 2014 the destruction of crosses in Zhejiang, the 2018 Regulations on Religious Affairs, the closure of Beijing’s Zion Church and Chengdu’s Early Rain Covenant Church, and the nine-year sentence given to pastor Wang Yi in 2019 have placed both registered and unregistered churches under heavy pressure.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/belie: Conservative evangelical theology with strong emphases on the Bible, conversion, holiness and the imminent return of Christ, transmitted by revivalists and indigenous teachers rather than by seminaries.
The principle that Chinese churches must be self-governing, self-supporting and self-propagating, shared in different senses by independent churches, Three-Self and house churches.
In the house churches, the conviction that the church’s head is Christ, not the state, and that suffering is a normal mark of faithfulness.
Watchman Nee’s ecclesiology of one church in each locality and his teaching on the spirit, soul and body and the ‘inner life’.
Pentecostal-type expectations of healing, exorcism, visions and spiritual gifts, widespread in rural networks and in the True Jesus Church.
In the Three-Self Movement, ‘love country, love church’ and K. H. Ting’s project of theological reconstruction emphasising God’s love over the believer–unbeliever divide.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/strat: Self-supporting independent congregations and federations, starting with the Chinese Christian Independent Church in 1906.
Itinerant revival campaigns with evangelistic bands and witness teams that continued after the evangelist left.
Lay-led meetings in homes, with itinerant evangelists, hand-copied Scripture and short-term training classes during times of persecution.
Networks of house churches with their own training schools, sending ‘workers’ from Henan and Anhui to other provinces.
State-registered churches, seminaries and Bible printing (Amity Press) within the framework of the Three-Self Movement.
Overseas Chinese networks in Southeast Asia, Taiwan and North America that carried revival preaching and literature beyond China.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/group: Rural Han Chinese villagers in Henan, Anhui, Shandong and Zhejiang, who became the core of the house-church networks.
Urban intellectuals, students and professionals, among whom ‘urban house churches’ multiplied after the 1990s.
Overseas Chinese in the Philippines, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Taiwan through John Sung and other revivalists.
Wenzhou entrepreneurs, whose business networks spread churches across China and to Europe.
Chinese migrant workers in coastal factory cities.
Some minority peoples (Lisu, Miao, Yi) whose churches, founded by missions, became wholly indigenous after 1950.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/chall: The identification of Christianity with Western imperialism, the unequal treaties and the anti-Christian movements of 1900 and 1922–27.
War with Japan and civil war (1937–49), which disrupted churches across the country.
Persecution under Communist rule: accusation campaigns, long imprisonments and the total closure of churches in 1966–79.
The division between registered and unregistered Christians, marked by mutual suspicion and theological disagreement.
A shortage of trained pastors relative to the rapid growth of believers after 1979.
Since 2018, renewed restrictions on online worship, youth ministry, foreign contacts and church buildings.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/harms: Three-Self accusation campaigns of the early 1950s compelled Christians to denounce missionaries and fellow believers, leaving lasting wounds and mistrust.
Rival claims of orthodoxy between registered and unregistered churches have led to mutual condemnation and, at times, to reporting fellow Christians to the authorities.
Poorly taught rural networks proved vulnerable to heterodox movements such as Eastern Lightning (Church of Almighty God), which has used deception and coercion against house-church members.
Exaggerated statistics and dramatic testimonies published by some Western advocacy groups distorted perceptions and complicated life for Chinese believers.
Authoritarian leadership and personality cults in some networks and in Witness Lee’s later movement produced divisions and abuse allegations.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/devel: Proved that Chinese Christianity could survive and grow without missionaries, foreign funds or public church buildings.
Produced theological and devotional writings, especially Watchman Nee’s, that have shaped evangelicals worldwide.
Created a Chinese Christian hymnody, notably the Canaan Hymns of the house-church songwriter Lü Xiaomin.
Inspired missionary vision among Chinese believers through the Back to Jerusalem movement and overseas Chinese churches.
Showed how revival preaching, lay leadership and home meetings can sustain a church through prolonged persecution.
Through the registered churches, reopened tens of thousands of churches and printed many tens of millions of Bibles inside China.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/outco: Chinese Christianity became thoroughly Chinese in leadership and style and grew from about one million Protestants in 1949 to tens of millions, but remains divided between registered and unregistered churches and under tightening state control.

missions/chinese-indigenous-church/count: Independent churches from 1906, indigenous movements in Beijing, Shandong and Fujian, the Three-Self churches and the vast post-1979 house-church networks.
The True Jesus Church arrived in 1926; Witness Lee moved the Local Churches’ centre to Taipei in 1949; John Sung preached there in 1936.
John Sung’s campaigns of 1935–39 revived Chinese churches and left lasting evangelistic bands.
Sung’s preaching among Chinese Indonesians in Java and Sumatra founded influential evangelistic movements.
Sung’s campaigns strengthened Chinese churches in Manila and beyond.
Witness Lee moved to Los Angeles in 1962 and founded the Living Stream Ministry; Chinese diaspora churches multiplied.
Back to Jerusalem evangelists reached Urumqi, Hami and Kashgar in the late 1940s before the Communist victory stopped them.
A refuge for Chinese evangelists and publishers after 1949, and later a base for Bible distribution and church support in the mainland.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/journ: John Sung’s revival tours of Southeast Asia

Sung’s campaigns among overseas Chinese drew large crowds, emphasised confession of sin and formed small evangelistic bands of converts to continue the work; the stops shown are among many he visited.
The first Back to Jerusalem evangelists head for Xinjiang
Mark Ma, Simon Zhao and members of the Back to Jerusalem Evangelistic Band

Small teams walked and rode along the old Silk Road intending to evangelise westward to Jerusalem; the closing of China’s borders and arrests after 1949 ended the effort, and Simon Zhao spent decades in prison in Xinjiang.
Witness Lee carries the Local Churches to Taiwan
Sent by Watchman Nee to Taiwan as the Communists took Shanghai, Lee built the Local Churches there and later in the United States, while Nee remained and was imprisoned.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/relat: The Back to Jerusalem vision and overseas Chinese churches made China a potential, if constrained, sending church.
The China Christian Council joined the World Council of Churches in 1991, linking the registered church to the ecumenical movement.
Korean and Chinese-diaspora missionaries supported house-church training and Bible distribution after 1992, often informally.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/agree: Adopted (and transformed) Henry Venn’s three-self principle — self-government, self-support and self-propagation — as the charter of Chinese church independence.
House churches largely retained the CIM’s conservative evangelical theology, Chinese dress-and-language identification and expectation of suffering.
Shared the Korean church’s revival piety, early-morning prayer and lay leadership.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/disag: Independent leaders such as Wang Mingdao and Watchman Nee rejected denominational and missionary control, and the Three-Self Movement denounced the CIM and other missions as instruments of imperialism.
House-church Christians criticised the WCC and Western ecumenical bodies for partnering with the state-controlled Three-Self churches while unregistered believers were imprisoned.

Protestant indigenous movements repudiated the Catholic accommodation of ancestor rites, while the Catholic community itself split between the state-sponsored Patriotic Association and the Rome-loyal underground.
The True Jesus Church adopted Pentecostal practice but broke with Western Pentecostal missions, condemning them as false churches and adopting Oneness and Sabbatarian teaching.
missions/chinese-indigenous-church/devia: The Three-Self Movement’s political subordination to the Party’s United Front departed from the original missionary meaning of ‘self-government’, which had aimed at freedom from external control.

Witness Lee’s later teachings (e.g. ‘calling on the name of the Lord’ and the ‘mingling’ of God and man) were condemned in China as the ‘Shouters’ and debated as heterodox by evangelicals, though some Western evangelical bodies later affirmed the Local Churches as orthodox.
The True Jesus Church’s Oneness theology and claim to be the only true church diverged from historic Trinitarian Christianity.
Eastern Lightning’s claim that Christ has returned as a Chinese woman represents a complete break from Christianity that exploited house-church networks.
